items.titel: EU to ban Russian flags and teams at European sports events, in new sanctions round
items.anriss: Russian flags are to be forbidden at European sports events, in new soft-power sanctions, also accompanied by harder measures to stop European firms from helping rebuild Russian oil refineries.

absaetze.t: Russian flags are to be forbidden at European sports events, in new soft-power sanctions, also accompanied by harder measures to stop European firms from helping rebuild Russian oil refineries.

“We are introducing bans on Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag. We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols [at sports events],” said European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in a video-note on Monday (23 November), unveiling her proposals for the 22nd round of Russia sanctions.
“We will [also] introduce restrictions on Russians holding posts in governing bodies of European-based sports federations,” she added.

The sports sanctions come in retort to a decision by the International Olympic Committee in Lausanne, Switzerland, which said, in July, that it was acceptable for Russia to return to world sports, despite the Ukraine war.

The International Fencing Federation, the Executive Committee of World Gymnastics, the International Judo Federation, and the International Weightlifting Federation were among those who subsequently welcomed back Russians.

Von der Leyen’s proposed ban on Russian insignia echoes national bans on Soviet symbols in Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, as well as Nazi swastika bans in Austria, France, Germany, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia.

Her proposals against Russians heading sports federations would dethrone Russia's richest man, steel billionaire Vladimir Lisin, as president of the International Shooting Sport Federation in Munich, Germany, and Umar Kremlev, the boss of the International Boxing Association in Lausanne, since Switzerland automatically aligns with EU sanctions.
Kremlev became famous this year for bankrolling US president Donald Trump's son's lavish Bahamas wedding.
The EU also blacklisted Russia's former world chess federation boss, Arkady Dvorkovich, in June, for making pro-war remarks, prompting him to lose his post.

But if Putin's sports-washing seemed trivial compared to his daily killings of civilians in Ukraine, the EU Commission has also tabled a ban on European firms fixing the damage that Ukraine is doing with long-range drone attacks against Putin's oil infrastructure - a vital source of money for his war.

items.titel: Haiti: El Salvadors Präsident Bukele wegen Militäreinsatz gefeiert
items.anriss: In Haiti konnten auch internationale Missionen wenig an der grassierenden Gewalt ändern. Jetzt griff El Salvadors Präsident Bukele ein - mit mehreren Tausend Soldaten, ohne UN-Mandat. Und wird wie ein Volksheld gefeiert. Von J. Barke .[ …

absaetze.t: In Haiti konnten auch internationale Missionen wenig an der grassierenden Gewalt ändern. Jetzt griff El Salvadors Präsident Bukele ein - mit mehreren Tausend Soldaten, ohne UN-Mandat. Und wird wie ein Volksheld gefeiert.

Die Massen jubeln und tanzen im Kreis um ein Feuer, rufen im Sprechchor den Namen des salvadorianischen Präsidenten Nayib Bukele im Zentrum der haitianischen Hauptstadt Port-au-Prince. "Wir brauchen Frieden. Die Banden verschonen weder Unschuldige noch Kinder und alte Menschen, wir sagen: Lang lebe Bukele!"

Der in El Salvador autoritär herrschende Präsident stattet Haiti einen Besuch ab, nachdem er Ende Oktober über 2.000 Soldaten entsandt hat. Sein Ziel: Vier salvadorianische Soldaten retten, die während ihres UN-Einsatzes angegriffen wurden und seither vermisst werden, vielleicht ermordet worden sind.

Seitdem haben seine Soldaten sowie bewaffnete Roboter und Drohnen das Hauptquartier einer der mächtigsten Banden, der "400 Mawozo", und die Häuser zweier Bandenchefs zerstört. Dutzende mutmaßliche Bandenmitglieder getötet.
Haiti als Bühne für erneute Kandidatur

Inmitten seines Einsatzes lässt sich Bukele für die Präsidentschaftswahl in El Salvador im Februar für eine dritte Kandidatur registrieren - seine Erfolgschancen gelten als gut. Haiti wird für ihn zur Bühne. Hier zeigt er, was er zu Hause als Erfolgsmodell verkauft: hartes, schnelles Eingreifen.

Wir in El Salvador waren das gefährlichste Land der Welt, vor Irak und Afghanistan. Wir hatten eine Mordrate von bis zu 106 Morden auf 100.000 Einwohner. Wir wissen also, wie wir mit Kriminellen dieser Art umgehen.

Haiti ist das ärmste Land auf dem amerikanischen Kontinent. Nach UN-Angaben wurden etwa 1,5 Millionen Menschen durch kriminelle Banden vertrieben. Mit Morden, Entführungen und Vergewaltigungen terrorisieren sie die Bevölkerung.
Hoffnung in Haiti
Dementsprechend hat Bukele auf der Insel seltene Hoffnung geweckt - dass sich nach Jahren der Resignation endlich etwas bewegen könnte, obwohl mit seinem Einsatz die Gewalt weiter eskaliert.

"Wir verlangen nicht viel von der Regierung. Nur ein bisschen Sicherheit. Seit vier Jahren konnte ich nicht zum Champs de Mars gehen, nicht in den Süden Haitis fahren", sagt ein Haitianer der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters.

In Haiti selbst operieren zwar Polizei und Militär, haben allerdings laut Experten eine schwache Position. Daneben befindet sich eine internationale Sicherheitsmission der Vereinten Nationen, kurz GSF, im Land, der etwa 200 Soldaten El Salvadors angehören.
Hochsicherheitsgefängnisse nach El Salvadors Vorbild

Bukeles Einsatz mit Tausenden Kräften hat kein UN-Mandat, befindet sich also streng genommen in einer rechtlichen Grauzone. Von Haitis Übergangsregierung wird der Einsatz jedoch begrüßt - auch wenn haitianische Sicherheitskräfte die mangelnde Koordination kritisieren: Salvadorianische Gruppen sollen in gefährlicher Nähe zu den GSF-Truppen das Feuer eröffnet haben.
Am Freitag schließlich hat Haiti mit El Salvador ein Abkommen geschlossen: Nach dem Vorbild des berüchtigten Hochsicherheitsgefängnisses CECOT sollen drei Haftanstalten in Haiti gebaut werden.

items.titel: Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
items.anriss: The US president used his podium to attack the California governor for a decision to commute 548 death sentences.

absaetze.t: United States President Donald Trump has reaffirmed his support for the death penalty in an event that doubled as a platform to attack one of his most visible critics, California Governor Gavin Newsom.
On Monday, Trump spoke at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, where he was joined by the families of crime victims and his attorney general, Todd Blanche.
“The ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment,” Trump said of the death penalty, calling it a cornerstone of “ virtually every society throughout history, at least every successful society”.
“Under the Trump administration, we are bringing it back, and we will not stop in our pursuit of justice. We will not yield.”
He concluded the appearance by signing a presidential directive ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty in murder cases involving children, rape and human trafficking.
The directive also pushes for the attorney general to “expedite” executions for those on federal death row.

As part of his speech, Trump called on Congress to pass the Just Punishment for Murder Act, a bill sponsored by Republican Representative Brandon Gill, which the president said would “strengthen the death penalty in America”.
But he dedicated much of his remarks to slamming Newsom, a Democrat widely seen as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race.
Newsom’s second term as governor will end on January 4. Under California term limits, he was ineligible to run again in the 2026 midterm elections.
Still, the governor and former San Francisco mayor has carved a national profile for himself as a proxy for Democrats during high-stakes political campaigns — and as a critic of Trump.
Trump, however, zeroed in on one of Newsom’s final major actions while in office: commuting the sentences of those on California’s death row.
On November 5, two days after the midterms, Newsom announced that the 548 people sentenced to death in California would instead be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.
He described the action as an extension of the moratorium on executions he put in place after taking office in 2019.
“I could not remain true to my values and oversee the killing of people with death warrants in California,” he wrote in an open letter.
He nevertheless denounced the harm the 548 people had caused.
“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom wrote. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
He called on Californians to let the 548 people “die in obscurity” while remembering their victims.
Trump, however, framed the mass commutation as an effort to help “evil monsters” escape justice.

“This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said.
The president proceeded to launch barbs at Newsom, calling him “ a terrible governor” who “ stole away the only closure” the victims’ families “might ever have”.
He then invited several family members on stage to denounce Newsom’s decision.

“ You took the only justice we had and left families feeling abandoned by the state that promised to protect us,” Sandra Friend, the mother of eight-year-old murder victim Michael Lyons, said in her remarks, directed at Newsom.
In anticipation of Monday’s news conference, Newsom also released statements from families that supported his choice.

“When victims are this divided, the death penalty shouldn’t be the answer. Victims deserve so much more than a promise of justice through vengeance,” Jess Nichol, the sister of murder victim Polly Klaas, said in one of the statements.
“They deserve counselling, medical care, financial support, and a justice system that helps them heal. I want something better for survivors: real, tangible support.”
The tit-for-tat between Newsom and Trump comes as support for the death penalty has slumped in recent years.
A November poll released by the research firm Gallup found that 49 percent of US adults support the death penalty, the lowest rate since 1971.
Opponents of the death penalty have frequently pointed to the prevalence of botched executions and the possibility that innocent people may be executed.

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, has found that approximately 202 people formerly on death row were later found to be wrongfully convicted. The exoneration rate, it said, was one for every eight people executed in the US.
Death penalty cases also typically tend to result in longer court battles and higher costs.
Before Newsom’s mass commutation, California reportedly had the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, representing roughly a quarter of the country’s death sentences.
Newsom’s successor, Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, has pledged to continue the death penalty moratorium once sworn in.
But that policy puts California at odds with a push under Trump to embrace the death penalty and expand execution methods.
Upon taking office for a second term on January 20, 2025, Trump signed the first of several executive orders aimed at “restoring the death penalty”.
He pushed to have execution be the de facto punishment for the murder of law enforcement officers, as well as for murder cases where undocumented immigrants are the defendants.
In April, the Trump administration also said it would prioritise the use of the death penalty by expanding the acceptable methods for federal execution, including firing squads.
In October, Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that one execution by firing squad — that of the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan — would be livestreamed to the public, prompting backlash.
Trump later walked back the announcement, amid reports that he did not realise Hassan was in a wheelchair.
During his first term, Trump oversaw 13 federal executions, the most of any president in decades. In Monday’s speech, he framed such punishments as “common sense”.
“ When it comes to defending the lives and safety of American people, there can be no compromise,” he said.

items.titel: Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict
items.anriss: Despite rising enrolment, violence, displacement and poverty keep children out of school in northeastern state.

absaetze.t: Maiduguri, Nigeria – During years of Boko Haram violence, Maryam Umar’s school in Baga, a town in northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, was forced to close as violence displaced families and disrupted education across the region.
The closure of the Higher Islamic College in Baga in the Kukawa Local Government Area was part of a wider crisis that deprived thousands of children of regular schooling.

With educational activities now resuming, Umar, a teacher, welcomed efforts to reopen schools and provide learning materials, telling Al Jazeera that the interventions were helping restore education in communities devastated by years of conflict.
Across Borno, authorities said school enrolment has risen sharply as damaged classrooms are repaired and families are encouraged to send their children back to school.
Enrolment in public and private schools reached 1,418,279 learners in 2025, up from 766,551 during the 2017-2018 academic session, according to the state government.

Yet officials estimated that almost 800,000 children remain out of school, highlighting the challenges facing a state where more than a decade of conflict has displaced communities and devastated public services.
The figures suggest progress in expanding access but reveal little about regular attendance, teaching quality or whether children who have missed years of education are catching up.
Rebuilding after years of violence
Borno has been at the centre of Boko Haram violence since the armed group launched its campaign in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.

Schools were among the institutions affected as attacks, displacement and a prolonged lack of security forced families to abandon their homes. In some communities, education became impossible as classrooms closed and teachers and pupils fled.
The state government has made school reconstruction a priority, building new facilities and rehabilitating classrooms damaged by conflict and flooding.

“In response, our administration has constructed 104 new schools and rehabilitated 2,931 classrooms and related facilities,” Governor Babagana Umara Zulum said during the commissioning of educational projects in Maiduguri in March.
According to the governor, the estimated number of out-of-school children has fallen from about 2.2 million at the height of the crisis to fewer than 800,000.
Borno Commissioner for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Lawan Abba Wakilbe said the increase in enrolment reflects renewed confidence among parents.
But increased enrolment does not necessarily mean children are attending regularly or receiving the support they need after years of disrupted learning.
The available figures also provide little indication of whether the supply of qualified teachers and learning materials has kept pace with the growing number of pupils.
A generation returning to classrooms

For 12-year-old Fatima Mahmud Umar, a student at the Junior Secondary School One in Maiduguri, education offers an opportunity to pursue ambitions that years of violence have threatened for children across Borno.
Wearing a blue and white chequered hijab and her school uniform, Fatima spoke to Al Jazeera about her hopes for the future.
She expressed gratitude to her parents for supporting her education and said she hopes to become a good ambassador for her community.
Fatima also welcomed government investment in schools, including efforts to support both Islamic and Western education.
But many children across Borno have yet to regain access to regular schooling.
Violence, displacement and poverty continue to create obstacles, particularly for families struggling to rebuild their lives after years of upheaval.

Even where schools have reopened, children who missed months or years of lessons may struggle to catch up with their peers while teachers must accommodate pupils with widely different levels of preparation.
For returning students, enrolment is only the first step. Their prospects also depend on whether schools can provide the support needed to help them progress.
Rural communities left behind
The challenge is particularly pressing in rural communities, where distance, violence and limited resources can make regular schooling difficult.
In the Gubio Local Government Area, residents have raised concerns about children who remain outside formal education despite the government’s reconstruction efforts.
Bukar Abdullahi, 49, highlighted the need to enrol more children during a town hall meeting in Gubio.
While commending the state government for investing in education, Abdullahi drew attention to the difficulties facing rural communities.
For families living far from functioning schools, distance can remain an obstacle. Financial pressures and concerns about safety may also affect decisions about whether children attend.
Although the government’s figures suggest improved access, they do not show how evenly progress is distributed between urban centres and rural communities.
Addressing those disparities will require more than classrooms. Schools also need qualified teachers, learning materials and measures to help families keep their children enrolled.
Expanding Islamic education
Alongside conventional schools, Borno authorities are seeking to widen educational opportunities through Arabic and Islamic institutions.

Through the Borno State Arabic and Sangaya Education Board, the government is working to integrate aspects of traditional Islamic learning into a system offering recognised qualifications and pathways to further study.
The establishment of Higher Islamic Colleges is part of that effort.
“This intervention reflects our commitment to building an inclusive education system that integrates spiritual development with academic and vocational advancement,” Zulum said.
According to the governor, the institutions follow a curriculum approved by the National Board for Arabic and Islamic Studies that allows students to pursue recognised qualifications.

The initiative aims to expand opportunities for children whose families favour Islamic education, but its impact will depend on whether institutions can reach underserved communities and provide adequate teaching and resources.
Beyond enrolment figures
More recent government statistics indicate further expansion of Borno’s education system although differences in the categories counted make direct comparisons difficult.
The state’s annual school census, released in September, recorded 1,801,295 learners across the wider education sector.
Separately, enrolment in public primary and secondary schools stood at about 1.3 million during the 2025-2026 academic session.
Those figures cover different categories from the 1,418,279 learners recorded across public and private schools in 2025 and cannot be directly compared to establish the precise rate of growth.

The government’s estimate that nearly 800,000 children remain out of school also requires context. Without consistent information on the age groups and methodology used, the reported decline from 2.2 million cannot be independently assessed from the figures provided.
Beyond enrolment, questions remain about attendance, teacher availability and learning outcomes, particularly for children whose education was interrupted by conflict.

For teachers such as Umar in Baga, the resumption of educational activities marks a change from the years when violence forced schools to close. For children such as Fatima in Maiduguri, access to education offers opportunities that years of violence have threatened to take away.
But for the hundreds of thousands still outside classrooms, Borno’s educational recovery remains unfinished.
For Wakilbe, the increase in enrolment is nevertheless a sign that families are beginning to regain confidence in the education system.

“When you look at where we started, 766,551 learners in 2017-2018, and see where we are today, this is not just a number. It is evidence that parents and communities once again trust our schools with their children’s future,” he said.

items.titel: Visegrád Four leaders voice concerns over EU budget proposal
items.anriss: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said his government did not consider the proposal an acceptable starting point for negotiations.

absaetze.t: Published on 23 November 2026 - 23:43 GMT+1

The prime ministers of the Visegrád Four (V4) countries voiced concerns over the European Union's next seven-year budget proposal at a meeting in Bratislava on Monday, questioning spending priorities and plans to include funding for Ukraine.
ADVERTISEMENT
The leaders were meeting with the Austrian chancellor in Slovakia to discuss economic cooperation, migration and the draft of the budget.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said his government did not consider the proposal an acceptable starting point for negotiations.

He said he had therefore written to European Council President António Costa to explain that he saw little point in holding a special council meeting scheduled for later in the week as "there is no point spending two days in Brussels not agreeing on anything."
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also signalled his concerns over the proposed budget, saying he had expected the European Commission to show at least some sign that it wanted to save money.
He argued that maintaining a European Parliament in three locations was unnecessary and costly, while also voicing concerns over member state contributions.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, who hosted the meeting, said the leaders had not adopted a joint position on the budget during Monday's meeting, as this had not been the purpose of their discussions, although he noted that they were broadly aligned on the subject.
Funding for Ukraine

For his part, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke mainly about security, saying that Poland was committed to peace but that recent events showed the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine on Poland.
Tusk underlined the importance of continuing support for Kyiv, arguing that the country's ability to defend itself was of strategic significance for Europe's security.
However, his Hungarian counterpart, Magyar, warned that "support for Ukraine should not be included in the EU budget."
Magyar said there was no question that Ukraine deserved solidarity and noted that Hungary was already providing various forms of assistance to the Ukrainian people and government.
But he argued that financial support for Ukraine should not be incorporated into the bloc's budget in a way that would make contributions mandatory for all members.

On the same issue, Tusk said he did not think it was a good idea for the EU to finance support for Ukraine through joint borrowing - something the Hungarian government has already made clear that it would not take part in.
At a press conference after the meeting, the leaders stressed that regional cooperation was not only important but also achievable, given their shared positions on a number of key issues.
Fico said the V4 countries and Austria broadly agreed on key issues affecting the region, including cohesion policy, migration policy and agricultural strategies.

One of the main topics was how to deal with illegal migration. All the leaders called for strict rules and their consistent enforcement, while Fico also praised a plan for some EU member states to establish immigration return hubs in Rwanda.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said it was in Austria's interest to cooperate with its neighbours and that he wanted the country to be an ally of the V4.
He added that closer cooperation would also help ensure that the rest of the EU better understood developments in central and eastern Europe and the strategic priorities shaping the region.

items.titel: Did Ukraine Use A Mothership To Launch Its Sea Drone Attack On Russian Ships in Benghazi?
items.anriss: The uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that attacked a Russian Navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday were launched from a mothership at sea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) claimed on Monday . The SBU’s comments appear to be the …

absaetze.t: The uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that attacked a Russian Navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday were launched from a mothership at sea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) claimed on Monday. The SBU’s comments appear to be the first official confirmation that Ukraine has ever used a vessel to deliver USVs for an attack. Still, its statement doesn’t prove a mothership was actually used, as there is good reason for misdirecting with such a claim, but it certainly seems more probable than not.

The SBU account also conflicts with statements made on Sunday about the origin of the attacks. Libyan officials claimed that the strikes were launched from a base in their country, while there were also claims, later denied, that the USVs sailed from Albania. For years, we have raised the possibility that Ukraine was using motherships to launch USVs, especially in the Black Sea. In the case of the Benghazi attacks, we directly mentioned that the strikes could have originated from a ship as opposed to the shore.
New Details On The Benghazi Sea Drone Attacks

As we reported yesterday, the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Merkury sank after being struck by USVs while moored at a dock in the port of Benghazi. A cargo ship was also struck by USVs while in the waters outside of Benghazi.
The SBU provided new details on Monday about these attacks.

“The Defense Forces of Ukraine conducted a unique special operation targeting two Russian military assets near the Libyan port of Benghazi,” the SBU reported on its website. “The targets included the sanctioned dry-cargo vessel MV Angara, used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multi-purpose corvette Merkury, which regularly escorted hostile naval convoys—including the MV Angara.”

“Both vessels constituted legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they directly supported the Russian Federation’s military capabilities,” SBU added. “The operation involved seven Ukrainian-made uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), which were transported to the designated location and launched from a ‘mothership.’ Despite the enemy’s attempts to destroy the Ukrainian drones from the air, sea, and land, the Security Service’s USVs reached their objective, located the targets, and struck them.”

The attack “resulted in the destruction of the Russian multi-purpose corvette Merkury (hull number 734), a Project 20380 vessel. Seeking refuge within the port proved futile. The ship was part of the Russian Navy and assigned to the aggressor state’s Black Sea Fleet; it had entered service in 2023. A multi-role Ka-27 helicopter was also on board the corvette and went down with the ship.”

The second target “was the Russian dry-cargo ship MV Angara (IMO 9179842), which was used to support Russian military logistics—specifically as part of the so-called ‘Syrian’ and ‘Libyan Express’ operations. The Defense Forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea. Such unique special operations undermine the enemy’s logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay the price for its aggression, even at a strategic distance from Ukraine.”
The SBU did not say where the so-called mothership was located or what kind of vessel it was.

In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky included an SBU video with a sea drone’s view of a massive explosion on the corvette. The sea drone then approaches the Merkury amidships on the port side before the view cuts to a large ball of fire seen from another sea drone. The ship appears to be approached by a third sea drone, but it is unclear what happened because the video cuts away to a distant view of the ship engulfed in flames.
The video also shows a sea drone approaching the Angara, striking it on the port stern. An aerial view then shows the ship in flames.
On Sunday, it was reported that the cargo ship struck was the Ascalon, which looks similar to the Angara.
Now a day after the attacks, Libya has closed off the section of the port where Merkury was sunk by lining up small boats to block the approach from inside the harbor.

After the initial attacks by Ukrainian USVs years ago, Russia placed layers of barriers across its harbor entry points and around its vessels. These fortifications grew more elaborate with time. The Kerch Bridge received similar passive defenses for protection. Today, these sort of measures are more commonplace globally.
The following video shows a Ukrainian USV being stopped by booms placed across Sevastopol harbor in 2023.

The total lack of basic passive force protection measures in Benghazi is something TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway highlighted on X. This clearly made Merkury a juicy target for Ukrainian clandestine elements operating in the Mediterranean.
Competing Claims

As we mentioned in the opening of this story, yesterday The Associated Press reported that the USVs were “launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.” The wire service cited an initial investigation into the attack. However, we noted at the time that we could not confirm whether the attacks came from the land or a vessel.

There was also a claim made by the Clash Report that the USVs were instead launched from Albania, which is about 530 miles north of Benghazi. However, Albanian officials quickly and vociferously denied that.

“We have taken note of reports alleging that the naval drone attack against a Russian corvette originated from Albanian territory. The reports in question are inaccurate and do not reflect the facts,” the Albanian Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs posted Monday on X. “Albania was not involved in this incident, and its territory was neither used nor made available for the launch or facilitation of such an attack. We categorically reject these allegations, which have been presented without verifiable evidence. We call on those responsible for disseminating them to correct the record and to exercise accuracy, due diligence and responsibility when reporting on matters of such sensitivity.”

Despite the discrepancies, one thing is clear. It is nearly impossible for Ukraine to have launched the attacks on Benghazi from its own shores. The Libyan port city is located roughly 1,300 miles from the nearest point where Ukraine could put a USV in the water. The USVs would have had to travel across the Black Sea, through the Bosporus, into the Aegean and down to Benghazi across the central Med. And it’s not like anyone is claiming this is what occurred. Clearly, the drone boats were launched far closer, likely from a ship operating in the Mediterranean, and in an area Ukraine has known to be operating in for years when it comes to clandestine attacks against Russian naval interests.
Based on imagery from the raid, the USV used was a variant of the Sargan 3000. Naval analyst H.I. Sutton was the first to point that out.

In a September story about the first USV attack on another USV, we described the Sargan 3000 as “6.9 meters (about 22.6 feet) long, 2.2 meters (about 7.2 feet) wide, with an operational radius of up to 1,600 km (about 994 miles) and can carry a payload of 450 kg (about 992 pounds). It travels at an estimated speed range of 40-55 knots.”

It is interesting to note that in the SBU video, the USV attacking the cargo ship had at least two tubes on either side of the hull. We don’t know whether they were for weapons or some sort of countermeasure, such as for smoke dispersal.

It is possible that Ukraine is using the mothership claim as cover for its operations inside Libya or elsewhere in the region, which would be far more of a sensitive issue than having a vessel deliver the sea drones possibly from international waters. The reported presence of Ukrainian forces in Libya has been a major political issue between the two rival factions controlling the country.
Libya has been in a state of near-constant civil conflict since a NATO-led intervention enabled rebels to unseat and kill longtime Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Currently, the internationally recognized Government of National Unity (GNU) rules the northwest while the Libyan National Army (LNA), led by strongman Khalifa Haftar, controls most of eastern Libya.

Haftar is backed by Russia. On Monday, his government said the attacks violated Libyan sovereignty and called for an international investigation into “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts, or military units in western Libya,” according to AFP.

“They cited information suggesting Ukrainian forces might be present in ‘areas around Misrata, Zawiya, and other potential locations,’” the outlet reported. “The attacks on Russian ships are believed to have been coordinated by these units. According to local reports, similar special forces are thought to be operating near Tripoli.”
The Push For Motherships To Deliver Sea Drones And Other Uncrewed Vessels

TWZ first brought up the possibility that Ukraine could be using motherships to launch USVs in 2022 as Kyiv was initiating what would become a large-scale campaign using drone boats against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. As we have frequently noted, many successful Ukrainian USV attacks have been recorded against Black Sea Fleet vessels and facilities, forcing the general evacuation of Russian naval assets from occupied Crimea and to bases like Novorossiysk in Russia proper. These facilities have all come under attack since the force posture shift.

The U.S., China, Iran and other nations have operated elaborate motherships and some are developing even more advanced purpose-built craft as launch platforms for USVs, UUVs, and aerial drones. At the same time, you do not a need a highly specialized mothership to deploy small uncrewed boats. That can be done by anything from a fishing trawler to a small cargo vessel — and those kinds of ships have one big advantage, they can hide in plain sight. By using normal ships to launch attacks like this, they can come via surprise and the launch platform can continue on with its clandestine mission far from its home shores.
As for what Ukraine’s mothership may look like, we don’t know. But if it does indeed exist, it will very likely look like nothing special at all.
Contact the author: howard@twz.com

items.titel: $16 billion propulsion mega-contract posted in error, Air Force says
items.anriss: The Air Force is planning to award the $16.1 billion Advanced Propulsion Acquisition Contract, but has not yet done so, the service told Breaking Defense.

absaetze.t: WASHINGTON — The Air Force is walking back an award announcement it made in error for a massive contract vehicle worth up to $16.1 billion for propulsion work, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense.

On Nov. 20, the Air Force announced it had picked 58 companies for the service’s Advanced Propulsion Acquisition Contract (APAC), set to run through 2041. The program is structured as an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract, meaning the Air Force is not necessarily obligated to spend its full amount.

That award, published on the Pentagon’s daily contract roundup, was posted erroneously, an Air Force spokesperson confirmed today, though the service is planning to eventually award the contract. After the disclosure to Breaking Defense, the Pentagon subsequently noted the correction in the Nov. 23 list of award announcements.

“Once awarded, APAC will serve as an agile, enterprise-level contracting vehicle for propulsion requirements across all lifecycle phases, including science and technology, research and development, test and evaluation, production, sustainment, and modernization,” the Air Force said in a statement to Breaking Defense.

The Air Force additionally confirmed that a total of 58 vendors so far are planned for selection, and that an initial $1,000 disbursement to each will “support participation” in a post-award orientation conference for the winners.

“Future orders will be competed among the qualified vendor pool as requirements are validated and funded. Specific platforms, scope, funding, contract type, period of performance, and pricing will be established at the individual Delivery Order or Task Order level,” the statement reads.

The vendor pool from the Nov. 20 contract notice features a range of firms, from startups to established engine primes with different areas of propulsion expertise. And the award comes as the Air Force seeks new and more effective ways to power its existing and future platforms, from drone wingmen to large mobility aircraft.

The Air Force has recently tapped several vendors to open up options for different sizes of drones and missiles, and is also developing an advanced engine that could power future platforms like the F-47 stealth fighter.
UPDATED 11/23/26 at 6:23 PM ET to reflect the Pentagon formally correcting the contract announcement.

items.titel: If Ukraine can improvise its way out of tech dependency, why can’t Europe?
items.anriss: “Unprecedented” is how Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky described his country’s successful operation that brought down parts of the Kerch Bridge earlier this month. The connector between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea has been a …

absaetze.t: Affairs
November 24, 2026
4 Min Read
The lesson from Ukraine’s Kerch Bridge operation is clear: weaponising technological dependencies only makes countries more determined to break them. Europe should take note.

“Unprecedented” is how Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky described his country’s successful operation that brought down parts of the Kerch Bridge earlier this month. The connector between mainland Russia and occupied Crimea has been a key Ukrainian target since the start of the war, for both its strategic and symbolic importance to Putin’s rule.

It wasn’t just the Kremlin that Kyiv was sending a message to, however. What made the operation even more impressive is that virtually all of it was conducted using homegrown Ukrainian – and in two cases, European – drones and missiles. It did not rely on Starlink either. Ukraine’s access to the satellite system, which is run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has in recent weeks been throttled on multiple occasions, compromising the nation’s war efforts. With the attack, Ukraine showed that it also held cards – and did not necessarily need Washington to play them.

The episode is a textbook case of what countries can achieve when necessity breeds innovation. It also shows the downside of overzealously weaponising dependencies: those on the receiving end will be spurred to look for alternatives – and will eventually find them. Europe, which has also been working to reduce its dependency on US technology, would do well to learn from this example.

This is not the first time that Ukraine’s dependency on Starlink has proved fragile. In February 2025, in the lead-up to Zelensky’s infamous visit to the White House, the Trump administration reportedly suggested that Ukraine would lose Starlink access if it didn’t sign on to its disadvantageous critical mineral deal.

In response, European capitals rushed to find alternatives that they could offer Kyiv. They soon found that they had few on offer: Starlink, and its US military-governed version Starshield, remains by far the most mature and cutting-edge solution when it comes to this type of space-based connectivity. Europe’s own challengers in this domain, such as Franco-British Eutelsat, had long struggled to compete and lacks the reach to offer a like-for-like replacement. And scaling these alternatives would take time.

When Musk finally appeared to have made good on Trump’s threat this October, Europe was far from ready to fully fill the void, though it had made progress. With access to Starshield still restricted, Ukraine’s military has been relying on a patchwork of Eutelsat and other European solutions. For its attack on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine took an even more MacGyverian approach, deploying relay drones that were mounted with radios and modems. While these solutions are certainly no Starshield, they work on Ukraine’s own terms.

The 2025 Starlink incident became an important catalyst for Europe’s longer-term ambitions to become less dependent on US technology. The worry across the bloc is that meddling with Kyiv’s access could just as easily happen to Paris, Rome or Berlin. Tech sovereignty moved to the top of Ursula von der Leyen’s agenda – not just to ensure that Europe did not become economically vassalised to the US and China in areas such AI but also to remove the risk of such “kill switches”. Public opinion shifted too: a 2026 poll conducted by SWG and Polling Europe showed that 86 per cent of Europeans believe that the US could turn off critical internet systems.

Europe has fallen behind on developing its own competitive solutions in critical areas, such as AI and cloud computing, but it has also failed to adopt them when it has. It still too often defaults to shinier and more established US (and, increasingly, Chinese) solutions, meaning that homegrown challengers struggle to find customers and achieve scale.

Ukraine’s Kerch Bridge operation should inspire Europe to move past the rhetoric. For much of the war, Ukraine has relied on improvisation and incredibly clever use of the capabilities at its disposal to match a better-resourced adversary. Where access was restricted or at risk, Ukrainians have put significant effort into developing their own solutions.

The current geopolitical moment necessitates that Europe acts with this same sense of urgency and pragmatism. If the bloc wants more autonomy over its technology, it needs to accept that sometimes “good enough” will do the trick.
Katja Bego is the author of ‘Deep Connections: The Hidden Battles to Control Subsea Cables’ and a senior research fellow at Chatham House.

items.titel: Inside London Museum’s new Smithfield home: Secret vaults, a ghostly market and a bold vision
items.anriss: When architect Paul Williams first entered the site of the new London Museum a decade ago, it felt like walking into a time capsule. The old Smithfield General Market in the city’s central Farringdon neighbourhood had ceased trading 20 …

absaetze.t: When architect Paul Williams first entered the site of the new London Museum a decade ago, it felt like walking into a time capsule. The old Smithfield General Market in the city’s central Farringdon neighbourhood had ceased trading 20 years before. “There were the trolleys, meat hooks, ledgers,” he says. “Calendars marked. Life suddenly left and traders just moved out. There was a ghostly feeling of that presence still there.” He pauses. “It was very moving.”

Ghosts in the architecture remain today. Multiple levels of shops and offices around the market’s periphery have been removed but there are still the cavities where the beams that supported them once lay. The brickwork is blackened in places and tinged blue in others – vestiges of historic office partitions and wall coverings. The fireplaces have been removed, meticulously restored and then reinstated in their original positions; they hang high and spectral above the new ground level. Dwarfed by the cavernous space, they resemble iron postage stamps – relics of the market’s past life and history’s storytellers in its new one.

Given its purpose, the structure – part of a complex designed and built by architect Horace Jones between 1879 and 1883 – inspires an unlikely awe. The great, soaring dome in the heart of the ceiling evokes a cathedral-like reverence. Wrought-iron berries and leaves decorate the top of the Phoenix columns that dot the vast floor. Originally designed for fruit and vegetables, the space was repurposed as a place to sell fish, before becoming a meat market in 1898. For more than a century, this building was the heart of London’s meat trade: somewhere that came alive at night as crowds of men strung up sides of pork and heaved carcasses over their shoulders.

When Monocle visits in early November, Smithfield is once again bustling with activity. Bloodstained white coats have been replaced by hard hats and hi-vis; shanks and ribs with spirit levels and scaffolding poles. The project is designed by architecture firm Stanton Williams with collaborating architect Asif Khan and conservation architects Julian Harrap, and the site’s transformation from 19th-century trade hall into the biggest city museum in the world is almost complete.

When visitors arrive, they will likely enter on West Poultry Avenue, a street that has now been enclosed by the museum. Here, data about London will be shared in real time. On one side of the street is the Poultry Market, which will open as part of London Museum in 2028. On the other is the magnificent, domed General Market, home to the Our Time galleries, which display objects that pertain to living memory. Beneath it is the subterranean Past Time section, inhabiting what was once a railway goods depot that helped to streamline the market’s operations. Past Time tells the story of London from prehistory to 2012, when the city hosted the Olympic and Paralympic Games. A three-metre by six-metre window exposes the gallery to the passing Thameslink train on its way to Farringdon Station.
Display of objects from greyhound-racing track Harringay Stadium

In 2027 visitors will also be able to access a part of the museum that wasn’t in the original plans. It was widely thought that a series of Victorian storage vaults had been demolished at the tail end of the Second World War. Two years into construction, a contractor created an opening in an infill wall. “We shone the torch and it was our Indiana Jones moment,” says Williams. “We saw this amazing vault. It was very dirty, with one or two little creatures moving around – but you could see the barrel vault above.”

Once the space was opened, 800 sq m of barrel-vaulted rooms revealed themselves. Sitting seven metres under the museum, they are roughly at Roman street level, while the vaults’ jack arches are tipped with white-gold bricks that once helped porters to find their way in the dark.

The first iteration of London Museum opened in 1912 in the state apartments of Kensington Palace. In the following decades, it moved into a mansion house and returned to Kensington Palace. Then, in 1976, the museum launched as an amalgamation of two institutions in a purpose-built – and famously hard-to-find – building within the Barbican complex in the City of London. One of the museum’s longest-serving members of staff, chief technician Cliff Thomas, has been at the institution since its final days at the palace. The latest (and hopefully final) relocation of the museum is something of a homecoming. Thomas’s father worked as a clerk and then in personnel for Swift and Company out of Smithfield.

As a child, Thomas had the run of the market during his school holidays. “When I was about eight years old, one of the crews took me down into the freezers,” he says. “I was in my school uniform – shorts, mac, cap and long woolly socks, whereas they were all done up like Michelin men with their padding. Within two minutes, I was freezing and they had to drag me back out.”
The museum’s chief technician, Cliff Thomas

Smithfield market tells its own story of London – of architecture, commerce and labour – and it now houses objects from London Museum’s seven-million-strong collection that each, in their own way, do the same: from Neolithic-era polished-flint axe heads and pointed poulaine shoes to the signs made to support the NHS during the coronavirus pandemic and a 1920s art deco lift from Selfridges department store. In 2017 the “Whitechapel fatberg”, a 250-metre-long, 130-tonne mass of congealed fat, wet wipes, oil and other detritus, was discovered blocking the Victorian sewers under the UK capital. Part of it was procured by London Museum. “I think that we broke museum standards and made history in collecting a great big piece of rancid fat,” says the institution’s ebullient director, Sharon Ament.

“We are always looking for objects that have some kind of human connection,” says Annette Day, lead curator for the permanent galleries – whether the contents of a blocked sewer, Roman artefacts or the original Morley’s chicken shop sign. Williams shares a similar sentiment. “We want visitors to feel something,” he says. “I just want people to be moved. I want them to come away feeling that they have been uplifted – not just by the stories being told but by the building too.”

In Great Expectations, Charles Dickens immortalises the open-air market that existed before Jones’s buildings. The novel’s narrator, Pip, “came into Smithfield, and the shameful place, being all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam, seemed to stick to me”. Dickens himself now lives on in the museum in the form of an oxblood leather armchair that once belonged to the writer. There is as much of the city in that chair as in the novel, its characters and its author. The grime, stench and carcasses might be gone but something of them endures in the city’s layers – and sticks to all of us Londoners too. When Ament is asked what makes the capital special, she clasps her face and starts to shake her head. “What a city,” she says. “What a city this is.”londonmuseum.org.uk

items.titel: Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City
items.anriss: Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

absaetze.t: Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.
“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.
“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.
“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.
“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.
The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.
However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.
“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

items.titel: Do readers really want books by committee?
items.anriss: As reported by Maia Snow in The Bookseller , Between Worlds is a new community-oriented imprint that “will publish fantasy, romantasy, dark academia, horror and dystopia as well as requests from members of the community.”

absaetze.t: A new imprint from Harper Voyager is betting they do.

As reported by Maia Snow in The Bookseller, Between Worlds is a new community-oriented imprint that “will publish fantasy, romantasy, dark academia, horror and dystopia as well as requests from members of the community.”

The new imprint was announced via an unboxing video on Instagram, with a caption explaining that Between Worlds “will be kind of like a book club! They will ask readers about their opinions and feedback! So for example, you have a say in what they publish and can even share which designs you prefer and what merch they bring out! ⭐️” All of the imprint’s decisions, from editorial through marketing, will be informed by reader choices, it seems.

Between Worlds’s own Instagram foregrounds the book club part of the project (“A fantasy community and imprint”) and describes their process, which will “use surveys, polls and community discussions to find out what you would like to read … and what you’re tired of! We then find those stories and work with amazing author, illustrators, designers, and booksellers to bring you your next reading obsession.” Community management will flow up through all parts of the process. Whether this works to produce sales or good books remains to be seen, but combining a membership model with publishing is probably a savvy way to boost sales, or at least guarantee a dependable floor on sales figures.

Between Worlds sounds similar to Bindery Books, which is also built around a full integration of members and influencers into the work of publishing. Bindery’s app caters to influencers, folding in affiliate sales and revenue sharing, along with the offer of a co-produced imprint: “Tastemakers with thriving communities have the opportunity to launch a branded imprint fully supported by Bindery’s in-house publishing team.”

I’m not the target audience here, but I don’t recognize any of Bindery’s titles. But I do recognize the types of titles they’re putting out. The vibe of a romantasy cover or a thriller cover is immediately legible: if this is the type of book you read, the cover says, here is another like it.

Again, this is probably a good sales tactic, and I’m not saying I’m above this sort of recognizable marketing. When I spot a book cover with an old painting and the title and author in a solid pastel box, I’m thinking “NYRB” and checking it out. And did I think about dressing as a Fitzcarraldo Edition for Halloween but couldn’t find the right shade of blue clothes? Ask me next October.

But directly integrating this kind of marketing branding into the editorial process strikes me as risky, and pushing things towards a hazy, bland median. And I imagine it will create a feedback loop that will drive their output in one direction. (That so much culture is feeling more generic isn’t just the fault of creative production underestimating audiences taste or capability to handle challenge—it also comes down, at least partially, to the audience itself.) Plus, the shift towards “you sell yourself a book” is another blow for the self-checkout-ification of industries, where labor downsizing and the offloading of work onto the consumer is packaged as choice and community.

I know I’m being naive about how creative decisions have long been made. I know that focus groups are nothing new. And Lord knows I spent enough years as an improvisor to know that art by committee can be great. But I also know that a majority of improv shows aren’t good—they’re bad, even—and that something profound or moving coming out of design by committee is rare. For every story like the movie Airplane! being sharpened by test audience reactions, there are many more Poochies and Europa Jeeps.

With books, giving readers the keys to acquiring new voices and new stories seems ironically risky to me, even though it’s likely motivated by a desire to hedge on editorial risk. A traditional editorial process doesn’t guarantee good books or bestsellers either, but asking a book club to prompt their dream novel introduces more questions for me: How do you maintain variety and diversity? How do you keep things from getting boring? And how will you find a book that will be genuinely surprising?

A memorable book is often the one that you didn’t expect—I’ve rarely been bowled over by something that delivered exactly on my expectations. Maybe these focus-grouped books, that are delivering on a set of wishes and packaged to look like the kind of book you already read, aren’t actually meant to be memorable or challenging books. Maybe they don’t need to be, and only have to exist within the continuum of a reader’s stated taste and preference. I see the logic in making the “customers also bought” section of every webstore into an editorial mission statement. But while not everything needs to be a transcendent experience, why not dream a little, and put resources towards those higher aspirations?
